_comment: Canonical historical periods for Explore Through Time browsing, in chronological order. A period page represents WHEN A LEGEND IS SET, not when it was written down. The record axis is carried separately by each legend's `earliest_record` field. Membership comes from a legend's controlled `period_slug` field, which holds exactly one of the slugs below or nothing at all. Nothing is a correct answer, and it is the right answer for undatable oral tradition. `bounds` are [start, end] years with negative values for BC; they overlap on purpose where viking-age sits inside early-medieval-britain, so read `disambiguation` before assigning. `match` is the legacy free-text `period` value, kept only as a bridge until period_slug coverage is complete. Full assignment rules are in content-style-guide.md under 'Assigning period_slug'. Generated by generate_pages.py into /legends/period/<slug>. Every period page is generated regardless of how many legends currently carry it, since this is a fixed historical framework rather than a curated collection.

periods.title: Prehistoric Britain
periods.disambiguation: Mesolithic and Neolithic only, before about 2500 BC. Long barrows, chambered tombs, causewayed enclosures and the earliest stone settings. A round barrow or a hillfort takes its own later period instead.
periods.overview: The millennia before written record in Britain and Ireland, from the first hunter-gatherers after the last Ice Age through the Neolithic farmers who raised the great stone monuments. No contemporary text survives from this era, so any folklore tied to it (the standing stones, barrows and hillforts still visible in the landscape) was necessarily invented long afterwards to explain features whose original purpose had been forgotten.

periods.title: Bronze Age
periods.disambiguation: Round barrows, stone circles, cairns and the buried-treasure traditions attached to them.
periods.overview: Roughly 2500 to 800 BC, the period of Britain and Ireland's first metalworking, extensive trade networks and monuments such as Stonehenge's later phases. Folklore attached to Bronze Age sites is almost always retrospective, imposed by later communities who no longer knew who had built the barrows, stone circles and hillforts dotting the countryside.

periods.title: Iron Age
periods.disambiguation: Hillforts, brochs, crannogs, druids and native deities. An Iron Age deity keeps this period even when the only surviving attestation is a Roman inscription, because the belief is what is being dated, not the stone.
periods.overview: From around 800 BC to the Roman conquest, when Britain and Ireland were home to Celtic-speaking tribal societies, hillforts and a rich, largely oral mythological tradition. Very little of that oral material survives directly (most is known through later Roman commentary or medieval Irish and Welsh manuscripts), but hillforts, ritual sites and votive deposits still anchor local legend today.

periods.title: Roman Britain
periods.disambiguation: 43 to 410 in Britain. Ireland was never a province, so Irish material of these centuries belongs in iron-age or early-medieval-britain. Traditions that narrate events under Roman rule belong here, including the Glastonbury Joseph of Arimathea legend.
periods.overview: 43 to around 410 AD, when Britain (though not Ireland) was a Roman province. Roman-British folklore often blends native and imported deities and features specific historical figures, roads, walls and forts as the setting for later legend, with Hadrian's Wall and sites along Roman roads especially rich in accumulated story.

periods.title: Sub-Roman Britain
periods.disambiguation: 410 to about 600. All Arthurian material belongs here, Vortigern, Merlin and Dinas Emrys included, because that is where the tradition places the events whatever century the text was written in.
periods.overview: The two centuries or so after Roman withdrawal, before Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were firmly established, a poorly documented era from which the Arthurian legend is traditionally supposed to spring. Written sources are scarce and often written centuries later, so this period is unusually thick with legend built on very little solid historical record.

periods.title: Early Medieval Britain and Ireland
periods.disambiguation: 600 to 1066 across all three countries: Anglo-Saxon England, early Christian Ireland, and Pictish and Gaelic Scotland. The Ulster and Mythological cycles belong here. Where the material is specifically Norse, use viking-age.
periods.overview: Roughly 600 to 1066, covering Anglo-Saxon England, early Christian Ireland, and the Pictish and Gaelic kingdoms of Scotland. These are the first centuries whose stories survive in something close to their own words. Irish monastic scribes wrote down the Ulster and Mythological cycles, and Old English poetry preserves wyrms, barrow-wights and night-monsters that were already old when the poems were made. Kings, saints and heroes of these centuries still have hills, wells and stones named after them across all three countries.

periods.title: Viking Age
periods.disambiguation: 793 to 1066, overlapping early-medieval-britain on purpose. Choose it only when the legend is about Norse raiders, settlers or Norse-derived belief. In Orkney, Shetland, the Hebrides, the Isle of Man and Norse Ireland it is the default for this window.
periods.overview: Roughly 793 to 1066, when Norse raiders, traders and settlers reshaped much of Britain and Ireland, especially the north and east of England, the Scottish isles, and coastal Ireland. Norse mythology and Norse place-names both left a lasting mark on regional folklore, especially in Orkney, Shetland and the Danelaw.

periods.title: Norman Britain
periods.disambiguation: 1066 to 1154, the Conquest and its immediate aftermath. Anything later in the Middle Ages is medieval-britain.
periods.overview: From the 1066 conquest through the 12th century, when a French-speaking aristocracy reorganised land, law and the church across England and, in time, parts of Wales and Ireland. Castles, monastic foundations and the earliest written Arthurian romances (via Geoffrey of Monmouth and successors) date from this era.

periods.title: Medieval Britain
periods.disambiguation: 1154 to 1485. Also the home of legends whose earliest and defining form is one specific medieval text with no independent setting of its own, such as Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
periods.overview: The broad high and late medieval period, roughly the 12th through 15th centuries, an age of castles, cathedrals, chivalric romance and the flowering of much of the folklore that later ages would treat as timeless. Many familiar legendary figures and ballads (Robin Hood among them) are first recorded in this period, even where the events they describe are set earlier.

periods.title: Tudor Britain
periods.overview: 1485 to 1603, spanning the Reformation, the dissolution of the monasteries and the reigns of Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. Religious upheaval left its own folklore (ruined abbeys, dispossessed ghosts) while the era's cheap pamphlet press first put many oral traditions, including several black-dog sightings, into print.

periods.title: Stuart Britain
periods.disambiguation: 1603 to 1714, taking in the Civil War, the Interregnum and the Restoration. Most English and Scottish witch-trial legends are set here.
periods.overview: 1603 to 1714, encompassing the Civil Wars, the Restoration and the height of the British witch trials. This is the period of Matthew Hopkins and the widest documented persecution of alleged witches in English and Scottish history, alongside a flourishing pamphlet and broadside tradition that recorded ghosts, portents and prodigies.

periods.title: Georgian Britain
periods.disambiguation: 1714 to 1837, Regency included. Smugglers, highwaymen and press-gang traditions cluster here.
periods.overview: 1714 to 1837, the era of the Enlightenment, the agricultural and early industrial revolutions, and a golden age of smuggling along Britain and Ireland's coasts. Antiquarian interest in the earlier past began in earnest during this period, alongside the first systematic folklore collecting.

periods.title: Victorian Britain
periods.disambiguation: 1837 to 1901. Use it for legends set in the Victorian period. Never use it for the far larger group of older traditions that Victorian folklorists merely wrote down.
periods.overview: 1837 to 1901, the height of industrialisation and empire, and also the great age of folklore collecting as a formal discipline. The word 'folklore' itself was coined in 1846. Spiritualism, ghost stories and fairy photography all flourished alongside a genuine anxiety that rural oral tradition was vanishing and needed to be written down before it was lost.

periods.title: Edwardian Britain
periods.disambiguation: 1901 to 1914. The same warning as victorian-britain, and it bites harder here: the Edwardian folklore-collecting boom recorded traditions of every age, and none of them belong on this page.
periods.overview: 1901 to 1914 (sometimes extended to 1910 or to the First World War), a brief but distinct era bridging Victorian certainty and the disruption of the wars to come. Its folklore is often a late flowering of Victorian antiquarian and spiritualist interests, including some of the best-known fairy photograph hoaxes.

periods.title: Modern Folklore
periods.disambiguation: 1914 to the present. For traditions that began in living memory. Never a holding pen for oral tradition of unknown age, which gets no period_slug at all.
periods.overview: From the First World War to the present, a period often assumed to be free of folklore, but which has in fact produced its own rich seam of urban legend, roadside ghost sightings, cryptid reports and reinterpreted older tradition. Modern media, from newspapers to the internet, now do much of the work oral transmission once did.
